summary:
Pasco has no documented trans-specific regional law, ordinance or enforcement pattern. The department stands under Peru's national framework, in which trans identity is not criminalised but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, repealed hate-crime protection for LGBT people from the Penal Code, and presided over rising recorded violence against trans women.

On 20 February 2025 the congressional Comisión de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, prohibiting any person from entering public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex. The text carries narrow exceptions for custody situations and for cases where entry is required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities, and obliges venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs. On 2 April 2025 the plenary approved the fused text of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de niños y adolescentes and waived a second vote; Article 5.1 bars entry into or use of public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than a person's birth sex. The trigger recorded for the bills was a July 2023 complaint about gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chávez international airport.

The April 2025 law also determines restroom entry by 'biological sex', which bars trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity, and its legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. Enforcement reaches daily life: activist Gianna Camacho argues the measure would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender. A consumer-protection body, INDECOPI, had already dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit under Resolution 0735-2022, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI.

The IDEHPUCP institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in legal analysis dated 15 April 2025 by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. The same analysis records that gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive, and that dehumanising comparisons were made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Hostility extends into broadcast media. Television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained as well. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
tangentialFactors:
Pasco's scoring rests on national legislation and national enforcement practice, so the department's profile is an indicator of framework exposure rather than of locally enacted rules. Nothing in the inventory records a Pasco ordinance, a Pasco authority applying the restroom restriction, or a Pasco-specific act of violence against a trans person.

The restriction's reach is illustrated by developments outside Pasco: the dismissal of a trans woman's complaint against a gym in Lima and the televised instruction to a member of Congress to use the men's room both show the policy operating in private commercial and media settings as well as in state facilities.

Regional comparison places Peru alongside Paraguay and Guyana as the only South American states without LGBT coverage in hate-crime law, while Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 obliges states in the inter-American system to guarantee trans people's full rights. The December 2025 sentence in the Azul Rojas Marín case is the region's first torture-by-discrimination ruling.

Recorded violence figures understate incidence, according to the 2024 report's co-author, so the 54 killings recorded between 2020 and 2023 should be read as a floor rather than a total.
localsOnly:
Residents of Pasco live under the national restroom rule established by Article 5.1 of the April 2025 law, enforced in practice by private and public security staff who may consult the DNI to determine which facility a person may enter. Venues are required not to post ambiguous restroom signs, and the legislative package prohibits inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

Gender-identity recognition for residents remains a long, costly and invasive procedure in Peru, which shapes how documents, facilities and official interactions are handled. A discrimination complaint route exists through INDECOPI, but the SmartFit decision of Resolution 0735-2022 shows that complaints about restroom assignment based on the DNI have been dismissed there.

Healthcare settings improved in June 2024, when national health authorities removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official guidance. Legal challenge remains available to residents: an activist suit produced a July 2025 ruling by a Lima constitutional court striking down an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional.

Residents also face the raised obscenity minimum of four years and the article 4 prohibition on media and advertising content under the April 2025 law, which Human Rights Watch describes as a pretext for repression and scapegoating of trans people. The 2017 repeal of LGBT hate-crime provisions means victims of bias-motivated violence cannot rely on those Penal Code provisions.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents how the national restroom rule is applied within Pasco, which authorities or private venues there enforce it, or whether any complaint, sanction or act of violence against a trans person has been recorded in the department. That gap is unresolved rather than evidence of non-enforcement.

The inventory does not state whether the July 2025 constitutional court ruling against an anti-equality decree affects the April 2025 law or its Article 5.1, nor whether the January 2026 status of the dictamen of bills 6506 and 8457 differs from the position recorded on 2 April 2025. Both questions remain unresolved here.

The claim that recorded hate-crime figures are only a sub-registry is attributed to the 2024 report's co-author and has not been independently quantified in the sources provided. No official count of killings of trans people for Pasco or for the period after 2023 is sourced.

Whether inclusive signage actually displayed in Pasco has been removed or sanctioned, and whether the June 2024 health-guidance revision has been applied by facilities in the department, is not sourced.
